`TagUUID` in `src/flask/json/tag.py` (line 191) is the `JSONTag` subclass that handles `uuid.UUID`. It converts in both directions because JSON has no UUID type, so a UUID has to be written as a plain string and rebuilt from that string on the way back.

- **`check(value)`** returns `isinstance(value, UUID)`. `TaggedJSONSerializer` uses it to decide whether this tag applies to a value.
- **`to_json(value)`** returns `value.hex`, the 32-character hex string with no dashes. That is a JSON-safe primitive, and it is compact.
- **`to_python(value)`** returns `UUID(value)`. `UUID()` accepts that hex string, so the original object is reconstructed exactly.
- **`key = " u"`** marks the value. The serializer wraps the output as a single-key dict, `{" u": "<hex>"}`. On load, that key tells the serializer to call `TagUUID.to_python` instead of leaving the value as an ordinary string.

Without the tag, a UUID would either fail to serialize or come back as a plain `str`. The tag makes a session or cookie round trip return a real `UUID` instead of a look-alike string. The `hex` form and the `UUID(hex)` constructor are inverses, so no information is lost.

There is no dedicated async view class in Flask's source. The premise of the question doesn't match the code.

The only "async method view" is `AsyncMethodView(MethodView)` at `tests/test_async.py:30`, and it exists only as a test fixture. It sits next to `AsyncView(View)` at line 22 and is registered at line 76 with `AsyncMethodView.as_view("methodview")`. In `src/flask/views.py`, the only view classes are `View` and `MethodView(View)`, which is the base class that does the HTTP method dispatch. `MethodView` is not itself asynchronous.

The test class subclasses `MethodView` instead of implementing dispatch on its own because the framework doesn't split sync and async dispatch. One dispatch path handles both:

- **`MethodView.dispatch_request`** (`views.py:182`) looks up the handler with `getattr(self, request.method.lower())`. It falls back to `get` for `HEAD`, and asserts that a handler exists. It then returns `current_app.ensure_sync(meth)(**kwargs)` (line 191).
- **`ensure_sync`** decides at call time whether the handler is a coroutine function. If it is, it wraps it so it runs synchronously, using the `async_to_sync` support from the optional `flask[async]` extra. Plain functions pass through unchanged.
- **`View.as_view`** (around lines 110 and 116) applies the same `ensure_sync` wrapping to `dispatch_request` itself. Async views work whether `dispatch_request` is a plain function or a coroutine.
- **`MethodView.__init_subclass__`** (line 165) builds the `methods` set from whichever of `get`, `post` and the other `http_method_funcs` the subclass defines. It doesn't check whether they are `def` or `async def`. That is why `AsyncMethodView` needs no extra code beyond declaring `async def get(...)`.

So an async method view inherits from the sync `MethodView` because Flask is a WSGI framework and async support is an adapter layer. Method-to-handler routing, `HEAD`-to-`GET` fallback, `methods` inference and `as_view` are all independent of sync versus async. Only the final call goes through `ensure_sync`. A separate async dispatch base would duplicate all of that and give you two parallel class hierarchies to maintain.

`ScriptInfo` (`src/flask/cli.py:293`) takes both parameters because they serve two different callers. One is a developer who builds a custom CLI in code. The other is an end user who runs `flask --app ...` from the shell. `load_app()` (line 333) checks them in a fixed order.

**`create_app` (a callable)**
- It is for programmatic use. A developer writes their own `FlaskGroup(create_app=factory)` (`FlaskGroup.__init__`, line 566, stored at line 589). `FlaskGroup` then passes it into `ScriptInfo(create_app=self.create_app, ...)` (line 670).
- `load_app()` calls `self.create_app()` directly (lines 341–342). This skips import machinery, path handling and name lookup. The app can come from anywhere, such as a closure, a config-dependent factory or a test setup, and it doesn't have to be importable by name.
- It comes first, so an explicit factory in code always overrides the string-based options.

**`app_import_path` (a string)**
- It is for the command line. The `--app` option's callback (around line 445) sets `info.app_import_path = value`. The value is a string such as `module`, `module:name`, `path/to/file.py` or `module:create_app(args)`. A user can only give a string there.
- `load_app()` splits it on `:` with `re.split(r":(?![\\/])", ..., maxsplit=1)`. The negative lookahead keeps Windows drive paths like `C:\...` intact. It then calls `prepare_import(path)` and `locate_app(import_name, name)`. Those two functions work out the module name, adjust `sys.path` and find the app or factory (`locate_app` looks for `app`, `application`, `create_app` and `make_app`, per line 67 and the help text at line 459).

**If neither is given**
`load_app()` falls back to trying `wsgi.py` and then `app.py` in the current directory. If it still finds nothing, it raises `NoAppException`. This is the default for a project that uses neither `--app` nor `FLASK_APP`.

After loading, the result is cached in `_loaded_app`, and the debug flag is applied if `set_debug_flag` is set. Later calls return the cached app. So the two parameters are two ways to do one job. The callable is for code that has the factory in hand. The import path lets the CLI find an app from a string.

`Flask.open_resource` (`src/flask/app.py:330`) and its blueprint counterpart `Blueprint.open_resource` (`src/flask/blueprints.py:104`) both reject anything other than reading. Each starts with `if mode not in {"r", "rt", "rb"}: raise ValueError("Resources can only be opened for reading.")` (`app.py:353`, `blueprints.py:120`).

The source doesn't state the reason in a comment. What the code and docstrings show is this:

- **Resources are read-only package data.** These methods open files relative to `root_path`, which is the directory of the app's or blueprint's package or module. That directory holds files shipped with the code, such as the docstring's example `schema.sql` or templates. They are part of the installed application. They may sit in a read-only or shared location, such as site-packages or a zip or wheel install. The app shouldn't modify them at runtime.
- **Writable data has its own method.** `Flask.open_instance_resource` (`app.py:363`) opens files relative to `instance_path`. Its docstring says: "Unlike `open_resource`, files in the instance folder can be opened for writing." Instance data (runtime state, local config, uploads) belongs there. Splitting the two methods means the mode, not the caller, keeps writes out of the code directory.
- **The check is a whitelist, not a blacklist.** `{"r", "rt", "rb"}` excludes `w`, `a`, `x`, `+` and every other mode, so no combination can slip through. It runs before `os.path.join(self.root_path, resource)`, so a rejected call never touches the filesystem.
- **The encoding parameter fits reading only.** `mode == "rb"` calls `open(path, mode)` with no encoding. The text modes pass `encoding=encoding`. Version 3.1 added the `encoding` parameter, which only makes sense for these read modes.

`ScriptInfo` (`src/flask/cli.py:293`) doesn't load the app in `__init__`. It sets `_loaded_app = None` (line 331), and `load_app()` (line 333) builds the app on first call and caches it. The source doesn't say why in one place. The reasons below come from how the object is created and used.

**1. `ScriptInfo` is created before the app location is known.**
- `FlaskGroup.make_context` (line 657) creates it as the click context object. It passes only `create_app`, `set_debug_flag` and `load_dotenv_defaults` (line 670).
- `app_import_path` is filled in later, when click processes the `--app` option (`_set_app`, line 440: `info.app_import_path = value`). The `--env-file` and `--env-file`/`.env` callbacks (`_env_file_callback`, line 493) also run after construction and can change the environment the app depends on.
- Loading in `__init__` would run before any of that, so it would find the wrong app or none.

**2. Some commands must work even when the app can't be loaded.**
- `FlaskGroup.get_command` (line 609) looks up built-in and plugin commands first. Its comment says they "should be available even if the app fails to load". Only then does it call `info.load_app()`.
- `--help`, `flask --version` and `flask routes --help` should also work with a broken or missing app. An eager load would fail before click could dispatch any of them.

**3. Loading errors are handled at the call site.**
- `get_command` catches `NoAppException`, prints a red error and returns `None`.
- `list_commands` (line 636) prints `NoAppException` without a traceback but prints the full traceback for other exceptions, then carries on.
- An exception in `__init__` would leave no half-built object to fall back on.

**4. The app is loaded at most once, from several places.**
`load_app()` is called from `get_command`, `list_commands`, `with_appcontext` (line 397) and the run command (line 955). Importing an app runs arbitrary user code, so a second import could create a second app or repeat side effects. The `_loaded_app` cache (checked at line 338, set at line 371) ensures all callers get the same instance. Importing only when a command needs the app is also cheaper for the commands that don't.

So the lazy, cached design lets `ScriptInfo` be created first and configured later by click options. The app is imported only when something needs it, and every caller shares one instance.

The premise doesn't hold: in this repository, setting `accessed` has no effect on how fast the signed cookie string is produced. I found nothing in the code that links the two.

**Where `accessed` is set** (`src/flask/sessions.py`, class `SecureCookieSession`):
- `accessed = False` is the class default (line 72).
- The `on_update` callback (lines 78–80) sets `modified = True` and `accessed = True`.
- `__getitem__` (line 84), `get` (line 88) and `setdefault` (line 92) each start with `self.accessed = True`. It is an unconditional plain attribute assignment. That costs one store per call, with no branch, lock or I/O.

**Where `accessed` is read:**
- Only `SecureCookieSessionInterface.save_session` (line 351) reads it, at line 363: `if session.accessed: response.vary.add("Cookie")`. This is once per response. It only decides whether to add a `Vary: Cookie` header, so caching proxies don't serve one user's page to another. It is a correctness feature, not a performance one.

**Where the cookie string is produced:**
- The signed string comes from `self.get_signing_serializer(app).dumps(dict(session))` (line 387). It runs only after the early exits: the session is empty, or `should_set_cookie` returns false (line 383).
- `dict(session)` copies the contents. It doesn't call `__getitem__` or `get`, so it doesn't touch `accessed`. The serializer then serializes and signs the copy. Flask's `TaggedJSONSerializer` (`flask/json/tag.py`) and itsdangerous do that work.

**Conclusion:** The cost of `dumps` depends on the size and content of the session and on the signing and serialization work. The `accessed` assignments in the read methods add only a trivial per-read cost, which is negligible next to serialization. Whether they can be skipped isn't a serialization matter. Reads must always set `accessed`, because `save_session` needs it to emit `Vary: Cookie` when the session was only read. A conditional check such as `if not self.accessed` would cost about as much as the assignment it saves.

The registration mechanism is cheap, and I found nothing in Flask's source that would degrade startup performance when it is repeated across many blueprints. The cost is small and grows in a straight line with the number of filters.

**The mechanism** (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py`):
- `Blueprint.app_template_filter` (line 444) is a decorator. It calls `add_app_template_filter` (line 461) and returns the function unchanged.
- `add_app_template_filter` defines a closure, `register_template(state)`, and passes it to `self.record_once(...)` (line 475). Nothing touches the app at that point. The closure is only appended to the blueprint's deferred-function list.
- When `app.register_blueprint(bp)` runs, `Blueprint.register` (line 273) calls `make_setup_state` (line 321) and then runs the deferred functions. `record_once` (line 233) wraps the closure so it runs only when `state.first_registration` is true (line 241).
- The work itself is `state.app.jinja_env.filters[name or f.__name__] = f`. That is one dict assignment per filter.

**Cost when repeated across many distinct blueprints:**
- Each blueprint adds one deferred closure per filter, and each registration runs one dict store. For N blueprints with F filters, that is N×F trivial operations at startup, once per process.
- `first_bp_registration = not any(bp is self for bp in app.blueprints.values())` (line 316) scans the registered blueprints for each registration. Across N blueprints that is about O(N²) identity checks. For realistic N this is still negligible.
- The first access to `app.jinja_env` builds the Jinja environment. That is a one-time cost, and only the first blueprint pays it. It would happen at the first template render anyway.

**Where a real problem could come from:**
- **Name collisions.** Filters go into one shared `jinja_env.filters` dict, so if two blueprints register the same name, the later registration silently overwrites the earlier one. The result is a correctness surprise, not a slowdown.
- **A very expensive filter body.** That would slow rendering, not registration.
- **The tests.** The filter tests in `tests/test_blueprints.py` register a filter on a blueprint and render a template. I didn't find any timing or benchmark test there.

If you have a benchmark or profile showing slowdown, send it and I can trace where it comes from.

The test is `test_dotted_name_not_allowed` in `tests/test_blueprints.py:254`. It calls `flask.Blueprint("app.ui", __name__)` inside `pytest.raises(ValueError)`. It checks that the guard in `Blueprint.__init__` (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:198`) fires: `if "." in name: raise ValueError("'name' may not contain a dot '.' character.")`. The same constructor also rejects empty names at line 195, and `test_empty_name_not_allowed` covers that.

**Why Flask forbids dots:** the dot is reserved as the separator in nested blueprint names. The evidence in the code is:
- `Blueprint.register` (line 273) builds registered names as `name_prefix + "." + self_name`. The 2.0.1 notes at lines 292–294 say that nested blueprints are registered "with their dotted name". This lets different blueprints with the same name be nested in different places.
- `_split_blueprint_path` (`src/flask/helpers.py:628`) recovers the parent chain by splitting on the last dot: `"a.b.c"` becomes `["a.b.c", "a.b", "a"]`. Flask uses that chain to find blueprint-level handlers, such as error handlers and `before_request` functions, for a nested blueprint.
- `url_for("test.index")` uses the same dotted format (see `test_dotted_names_from_app`, line 264).

**Why the check is in the constructor:** if a blueprint could be named `"app.ui"`, its name would be indistinguishable from a blueprint `ui` nested inside `app`. Lookups by dotted name could then match the wrong blueprint or the wrong handlers, and `url_for` endpoints could clash. Rejecting the name when the blueprint is created makes the mistake fail immediately at the point of definition. Otherwise it would show up later as wrong routing or handler lookups.

The test confirms the guard stays in place, so a future refactor can't remove it without failing this test.
